title: Book of Matrices
subtitle: Dies known to this Chancery
_comment: Pages are typed, not free text, so a matrix plate draws the actual device and a polity plate draws the actual arms. Adding a page kind is a branch in reference_book.gd; adding a page is a line here.

pages.heading: Book of Matrices
pages.body:
Every seal die this office knows of, with the year each was cut and, where it applies, the year it was destroyed.

A die is a piece of metal. It is cut in one year and broken in another, and it can only have made a mark in wax between those two years.
pages.marginalia: Nine tenths of the work is on this page and the rest is looking things up. — R.V.

pages.heading: How a seal is read
pages.body:
Four things on the wax must match the die recorded here:

   the picture
   the writing round the rim, letter for letter
   the shape
   the colour of the wax

And a fifth thing, which is not on the wax at all: was the die still in existence on the day of the document?

Rubbing wears the writing away. Missing letters are written here as dots and count as matching. Wear is not dishonesty.
pages.marginalia: Four things on the wax and a fifth that is not on it at all. The fifth is the one they will quote at you afterward, and never once before. — R.V.

pages._pagination_note:
THIS LEAF EXISTS TO MOVE A PAGE, AND THE PAGE IT MOVES IS THE MOST IMPORTANT COMPARISON IN THE BOOK.

ReferenceBook pairs pages as (spread*2, spread*2+1). Before this leaf, thurn_dietrich_i was page 5 and thurn_dietrich_ii was page 6 — so they fell on spreads 2 and 3 and COULD NOT BE SEEN IN ONE OPENING. Two cases turn on telling them apart: case_02 is the first die, dead since 1207, on a charter of 1213; case_04 is the second, alive in 1210, and is otherwise clean. Both are the same man, the same house and the same lion, and the difference is nine letters of legend and a pair of years — which was a memory test created by pagination rather than by the puzzle.

The book already proves it knows better one section later: wend_abbey and wend_chapter share spread 5 on purpose, and the second of them carries the marginalia that frames them as a pair. This does for Thurn what that already does for Saint Wend.

Anything inserted or removed above page 5 breaks the pairing again, silently, with every test still passing. Recheck the whole array after touching it.
pages.heading: Where a man has had more than one die
pages.body:
A die is cut for a man in a style, and when his style changes the die is cut again and the old one defaced. Both are his. Both are recorded here. Only one of them was on his belt on any given day.

So the question is never whose seal this is. It is which of his, and when.

The two that follow are the same man, the same house and the same lion. Read the legend letter by letter and then read the years.
pages.marginalia: The March is full of the old one, on parchment nobody disputes. That is the difficulty. — R.V.

pages.heading: Dietrich of Thurn — the first die
Dietrich of Thurn — the second
pages.marginalia: Two dies, one man, and the old one is on half the parchment in the March. Anybody wanting a Thurn seal has an impression to copy from and no die to copy it with. Check the year. Always check the year. — R.V.

pages._pagination_note: PARITY. ReferenceBook pairs (spread*2, spread*2+1), so inserting an ODD number of leaves above this point re-breaks every pairing below it — and the one below that matters is wend_abbey facing wend_chapter, which is the crook-versus-keys comparison case_03 turns on. Two leaves go in above; this is the second, and it is here rather than anywhere else because the section it closes is the one it is about.
pages.heading: When a die is broken
pages.body:
A die outlives its holder nowhere in this Empire, and in the March it does not outlive him by an hour. What follows from that is the whole of the test: after the day a man dies there is no die of his anywhere, and wax bearing his mark on a later instrument was pressed by something that should not exist.

The year a die was broken is written on its plate here. The day its holder died is written in the Kalendar of the Dead, in whatever house returned it. Where both books speak, read both.
pages.marginalia: The chapel at Thurnstadt and this book put Dietrich in the same year. Two sources in this office agreeing without being made to; I have seen it once. — R.V.

pages.heading: The Commune of Marchfeld
pages.marginalia: Never dead. Do not go looking for a break year on this one; there isn't one and you will talk yourself into something.

pages.heading: The Cathedral Chapter
pages.marginalia: Keys are the chapter. A crook is the house. They are not interchangeable and the abbey will write to you about it if you say they are.

pages.heading: The Wends of the Nether March
Of the Wends
pages.body:
They keep no seal. There is no die of the Nether March in this book because there is no die of the Nether March.

A Wendish grant is made by oath before named men in the place itself, and it holds for as long as those men live and can be found. When the last of them dies the grant becomes a thing that people remember, and after that it becomes a thing that people say.

Wax on a Wendish instrument was put there by somebody who knew that we would want to see wax.
pages.marginalia: The archive at Lenz burnt in '18 and took forty years of oath-rolls with it. Nobody has worked out yet what that means for the Nether March. It will not be pretty when they do. — R.V.
